question: What are the main steps of an end-to-end machine learning project?
expected_points: look at the big picture / frame the problem
get the data
discover and visualize the data
prepare the data for algorithms
select and train a model
fine-tune the model
launch, monitor and maintain

question: Why should you use stratified sampling instead of pure random sampling when splitting a dataset?
expected_points: ensures the split has the same class/category proportions as the full dataset
important when a category is small/imbalanced
pure random sampling could skew the test set

question: In the California housing project, what problem type is median house value prediction framed as?
expected_points: regression
supervised learning
single attribute (median_house_value) predicted from district features

question: What is a scatter matrix (e.g. pandas plotting.scatter_matrix) used for in data exploration?
expected_points: visualize every numerical attribute against every other
spot correlations and patterns
most ML algorithms ignore attributes with weak correlation

question: Why are attribute combination features like rooms_per_household useful?
expected_points: raw attributes like total_rooms are not meaningful across districts of different size
ratios/derived features per household or per capita correlate better with the target

question: What are the typical data preparation steps before feeding data to most Scikit-Learn algorithms?
expected_points: handle missing values (imputation or drop)
handle text/categorical features (encoding)
feature scaling (standardization or normalization)
feature engineering where useful

question: What is the difference between grid search and randomized search for hyperparameter tuning?
expected_points: grid search tries all combinations of a specified grid
randomized search samples a given number of random combinations from a distribution
randomized search can explore a wider space with a fixed budget

question: Why must data preprocessing transformers (imputer, scaler) be fit only on the training set, not the test set?
expected_points: avoid data leakage from test set into training
test set should simulate unseen data
transform the test set using statistics learned from training only

question: What should you do after launching a machine learning system in production?
expected_points: monitor performance regularly
sample predictions and evaluate them
monitor data quality / input drift
refresh the model on new data / retrain

question: For a classifier on an imbalanced dataset (e.g. 10% positives), why is accuracy a bad performance measure?
expected_points: a trivial classifier predicting all-negative gets ~90% accuracy
accuracy misleads when classes are imbalanced
use precision/recall/F1 or confusion-matrix based measures instead

question: What is the precision/recall trade-off and how can you adjust it?
expected_points: raising the decision threshold increases precision but lowers recall
lowering the threshold increases recall but lowers precision
threshold adjustable via decision_function scores instead of predict
choose based on application cost of false positives vs false negatives

question: What does the F1 score measure and when should you use it?
expected_points: harmonic mean of precision and recall
good single figure when you need a balance of both
especially useful for imbalanced classes
favors classifiers with similar precision and recall

question: What is a precision-recall curve and why is it preferred over ROC when classes are very imbalanced?
expected_points: plots precision vs recall at varying thresholds
area under PR curve summarizes trade-off
ROC can look overly optimistic under heavy imbalance because FPR uses negatives as denominator

question: What is the ROC AUC score and how should you interpret a value of 0.5 vs 1.0?
expected_points: probability the classifier ranks a random positive higher than a random negative
0.5 = random classifier
1.0 = perfect
compare classifiers on the same task

question: What is the difference between One-vs-All (OvR) and One-vs-One (OvO) multiclass classification strategies?
expected_points: OvR trains one binary classifier per class, rest vs that class
OvO trains a classifier for every pair of classes and votes
some algorithms (e.g. SVM) scale poorly with large training sets, so OvO is preferred for them
SGD/naive Bayes scale better with OvR

question: What is cross-validation and why use it instead of a single train/test split?
expected_points: split training set into folds, train/evaluate K times
gives a more reliable performance estimate
reduces variance from a single lucky/unlucky split
StratifiedKFold preserves class proportions

question: In error analysis of a multiclass classifier, what does the confusion matrix tell you?
expected_points: counts of actual vs predicted class per cell
diagonal = correct predictions
off-diagonal shows which classes get confused
symmetric patterns suggest systematic feature problems

question: What is multilabel classification and how does it differ from multiclass?
expected_points: each instance can get multiple labels simultaneously
multiclass = exactly one class among many
evaluation e.g. average F1 across labels

question: What are the two ways to train a linear regression model, and when is each preferable?
expected_points: closed-form Normal Equation
iterative gradient descent
normal equation works well for moderate feature counts, no learning rate
gradient descent scales to huge datasets / many features

question: What is the role of the learning rate in gradient descent and what happens if it is too small or too large?
expected_points: step size per iteration
too small = very slow convergence, many iterations
too large = may overshoot and diverge
learning curve of MSE per epoch helps diagnose

question: Compare batch, stochastic, and mini-batch gradient descent.
expected_points: batch uses the full training set per step (slow, stable)
stochastic uses one random instance per step (fast, noisy, can escape local minima)
mini-batch uses small random subsets (compromise, smoother than SGD)
all converge to roughly the same solution if learning rate decays

question: Why is feature scaling (e.g. StandardScaler) important for gradient descent?
expected_points: convergence is much faster when features have similar scales
with very different scales the cost function is elongated
SGD is very sensitive to feature scales

question: What is polynomial regression and what risk does a high polynomial degree introduce?
expected_points: add powers of features then fit linear model
can model nonlinear relationships
high degree can overfit training data
check with learning curves

question: How do learning curves help diagnose underfitting vs overfitting?
expected_points: plot train and validation error vs training set size (or epochs)
both plateauing high = underfitting (high bias)
large gap between train and validation = overfitting (high variance)
adding more data helps overfitting, not underfitting

question: What is the bias-variance tradeoff?
expected_points: bias = error from wrong assumptions (underfitting)
variance = sensitivity to small fluctuations in training data (overfitting)
increasing model complexity reduces bias but increases variance
generalization error decomposes into bias, variance and irreducible noise

question: Explain the difference between Ridge, Lasso and ElasticNet regularization.
expected_points: Ridge = L2 penalty, shrinks weights toward zero but keeps them
Lasso = L1 penalty, drives unimportant feature weights exactly to zero (sparse)
ElasticNet = combination of L1 and L2
regularization strength alpha controls penalty; alpha=0 recovers plain regression

question: What is early stopping as a regularization technique?
expected_points: monitor validation error during training
stop when validation error starts rising
save the model at the minimum
alternative to explicit regularization

question: What does logistic regression estimate and what is the softmax function used for?
expected_points: logistic regression outputs the probability of belonging to the positive class
uses logistic/sigmoid function
softmax extends to multiclass: outputs a probability per class summing to 1
decision boundary is linear even though the model is nonlinear in probability

question: Why might Stochastic Gradient Descent help escape local optima better than batch gradient descent?
expected_points: randomness/instability of SGD jitters the path
can jump out of shallow local minima and plateaus
gradually reducing learning rate (simulated annealing) balances escape vs convergence

question: What is an ensemble learning method and what is the wisdom-of-crowds intuition behind it?
expected_points: train and aggregate predictions of many base models (predictors)
a group of weak/erratic predictors can outperform any single one
aggregation reduces individual errors
e.g. Random Forest

question: How does a hard voting classifier differ from a soft voting classifier?
expected_points: hard voting = majority vote of predicted classes
soft voting = average of predicted probabilities, pick argmax
soft voting usually better when all classifiers can estimate probabilities
works best with diverse, uncorrelated classifiers

question: What is the difference between bagging and pasting?
expected_points: both train base estimators on random subsets of the training set
bagging samples with replacement
pasting samples without replacement
aggregation usually by voting/averaging; reduces both bias and variance

question: How does the Random Forest algorithm work?
expected_points: ensemble of decision trees trained on bootstrap samples
at each node split considers a random subset of features
aggregates tree predictions by voting/averaging
Extremely Randomized Trees additionally use random thresholds

question: What does feature importance in a Random Forest measure and how is it computed?
expected_points: average impurity decrease contributed by a feature across all trees
nodes using the feature weighted by how much they reduce impurity
Scikit-Learn exposes feature_importances_
useful to drop irrelevant features

question: How does AdaBoost work at a high level?
expected_points: boosting: sequentially train weak learners
each new learner focuses on instances the previous ones misclassified
increases weights of misclassified instances
final prediction = weighted vote of all weak learners

question: What is Gradient Boosting and how does Gradient Boosted Decision Trees (GBDT) fit residual errors?
expected_points: sequentially add weak learners, each trained on the residual errors of the current ensemble
GBDT uses decision trees as base learners
shrinkage/learning rate scales each tree's contribution
Stochastic Gradient Boosting subsamples instances per tree

question: What is stacking (stacked generalization) and what role does the blender play?
expected_points: train a final predictor (blender) on the predictions of base predictors
blender learns how best to combine base predictions
typically trained via cross-validated (out-of-fold) predictions to avoid leakage
can be multilayer

question: What are Random Patches and Random Subspaces methods?
expected_points: sample both training instances and features
Random Subspaces: sample features only, keep all instances
Random Patches: sample both
useful for high-dimensional data / sparse datasets

question: Why is diversity among base predictors important for ensemble methods to work well?
expected_points: ensembles aggregate predictions; correlated errors cannot cancel out
more diverse (uncorrelated) predictors make fewer collective mistakes
randomness (bagging, random features) injects diversity
mixing different algorithm families also increases diversity

question: Which performance measures would you use for a digit classifier on MNIST and how would you evaluate it properly?
expected_points: accuracy is fine here because classes are roughly balanced
cross-validation with StratifiedKFold
confusion matrix + precision/recall per class for error analysis
ROC AUC to compare classifiers

question: What are the main categories of machine learning systems?
expected_points: supervised vs unsupervised (vs semisupervised / reinforcement)
batch vs online learning
instance-based vs model-based learning
examples for each (e.g. kNN instance-based, linear regression model-based)

question: How should you choose a kernel for a Support Vector Machine, and what do the C and gamma hyperparameters control?
expected_points: linear kernel when training set is large or has many features
Gaussian/RBF kernel for complex/nonlinear boundaries; polynomial kernel also possible
C: soft-margin trade-off, larger C = fewer margin violations / more overfitting risk
gamma: RBF width, large gamma = narrower bell, more overfitting / decision boundary follows individual instances
scale features first (SVM is sensitive to feature scales)

question: What are the main weaknesses of decision trees and how can you regularize them?
expected_points: sensitive to feature scaling / rotation of data
high variance, prone to overfitting
instability: small data changes can give very different trees
presplitting vs postpruning; regularization hyperparameters like max_depth, min_samples_split, min_samples_leaf, max_leaf_nodes
cart algorithm uses gini or entropy impurity

question: How does PCA reduce dimensionality and how do you choose the number of components?
expected_points: centers data then finds principal components via SVD
components are orthogonal directions of maximum variance
choose d so that explained variance ratio reaches a threshold (e.g. 95%)
can plot cumulative explained variance vs number of dimensions
inverse transform reconstructs approximation; PCA is not good before a linear regression

question: How do you build and run a model in TensorFlow's graph-based programming model (TF 1.x)?
expected_points: first build a computation graph of ops/tensors
then create a session and run it (sess.run) to evaluate ops
placeholders feed data, variables hold model parameters
graph can be saved/restored with a Saver; can be visualized in TensorBoard

question: How does backpropagation train an artificial neural network?
expected_points: forward pass computes predictions layer by layer
compute loss (e.g. cross-entropy / MSE)
backward pass computes gradients of loss w.r.t. each parameter via chain rule
gradient descent updates weights
output layer activation depends on task (softmax for multiclass classification, logistic for binary, linear for regression)

question: What techniques help train deep neural networks successfully?
expected_points: proper weight initialization (He/Glorot-Xavier)
ReLU-family activations instead of saturating sigmoid/tanh (vanishing gradient problem)
optimizers beyond plain GD: momentum, Nesterov, AdaGrad, RMSProp, Adam
learning rate scheduling
batch normalization
dropout and other regularization to fight overfitting
reusing pretrained layers / transfer learning

question: What are the key components and advantages of convolutional neural networks?
expected_points: convolutional layers with learnable filters/kernels sliding over the input
stride and padding control output size
feature maps; each neuron connects only to a local receptive field
pooling layers downsample
far fewer parameters than fully connected layers; partial invariance to translation/scale; hierarchical feature learning

question: What is an autoencoder, what are its main applications, and what are common variants?
expected_points: undercomplete architecture: encoder compresses to latent code, decoder reconstructs input
trained by reconstruction loss; can learn features unsupervised (dimensionality reduction alternative to PCA)
stacked/deep autoencoders, tied weights
denoising autoencoders (corrupt input, reconstruct original)
sparse autoencoders, variational autoencoders (generative)

question: What are the core concepts of reinforcement learning as introduced in the textbook?
expected_points: agent interacts with environment, takes actions, receives rewards
policy maps states to actions
Markov Decision Process: state transitions and rewards
exploration vs exploitation dilemma (epsilon-greedy)
Q-learning: learn state-action values via Bellman optimality equation; Deep Q-Networks
